title: Pause
tagline: Designing friction that helps people scroll on purpose.
headline: Downloads went up 170%. So why did people quit in week one?
summary: I built Pause, an iOS app that puts a short puzzle in front of the apps you scroll on autopilot. Solo, with Claude Code as my engineering partner and analytics to show me where people quit.
outcomes: 10+ puzzles on one shared shell, plus seasonal themes
Downloads up 170%, mostly from a $500 Apple Search Ads test
Found the real leak: week one. D7 gate retention is 16%, the target is 30%
lessons: AI made building cheap. Knowing what's right is still the job
article:
I was spending 9 hours a day on Instagram. Screen Time limits got me down to one, but the limit sheet always had an "Ignore Limit" button, and one tap put me right back in the feed.

So I built Pause. It puts a short puzzle in front of the apps you choose. Solve it and you're in. You can still scroll; you just have to decide to.

I designed it, built it with Claude Code as my engineering partner, shipped it, and I'm still iterating. Downloads went up 170%. Then I found out people were quitting in week one. This is how I got from one to the other.

**Tools:** Figma, Claude Code, PostHog, App Store Connect, Applyra

## 1. The problem

Screen Time limits work right up until you need them. The pull is strongest exactly when you're worst at holding your own line, and the way out is one tap away. I knew I was doomscrolling and I did it anyway.

![One tap to bypass: the iOS Time Limit screen](content/pause/easy-to-bypass.jpg)

The question I kept coming back to:

> How much friction is enough to break autopilot, without making people feel punished or locked out of their own phone?

Too little and it's a toothless timer. Too much and people delete the app.

## 2. The first call: block it or slow it down

The obvious version of this app is a hard block: a timer that locks the app until it runs out. It's strong, but it feels like punishment, and people delete apps that punish them.

I went with a quick puzzle instead. It's enough to interrupt autopilot without locking anyone out. Opening Instagram becomes a choice you make, not a reflex.

## 3. Four rules I used to say yes or no

1. **A pause, not a punishment.** Warm gradients, soft glass and calm copy. No red warning screens.
2. **Not every app needs the same speed bump.** You set the difficulty per app, so the ones that pull hardest get a longer slowdown.
3. **One shell, many games.** The puzzles change and everything around them stays the same, so you learn it once.
4. **Don't collect what I don't need.** Analytics are counts only. Which apps you block and anything you type stay on your phone.

![Friction per app: the apps that pull hardest get the harder puzzle](content/pause/puzzle-difficulty.jpg)

## 4. The puzzle gate

This is where I spent most of my design time. The gate has to slow you down without turning into one more thing to fight.

### One shell for every puzzle

I started with Word Jumble and kept at it until it felt right. Then I wrote down what made it work and made that the rule for every puzzle after it:

- A blue to warm amber gradient with a faint scribble texture
- A top bar with the puzzle name and a close button
- A Young Serif title at 24pt with a quiet subtitle like "Round 1 of 3"
- 56×56 glass tiles with a 4pt radius, and a dark overlay on the active one
- A success haptic when you're right, an error haptic and a shake when you're wrong

Only the game area changes. That's why Sixdoku makes sense in a few seconds even the first time you see it, and it's how I got to 10+ puzzles without the app turning into a mess.

![Every puzzle in the same shell](content/pause/all-puzzles-same-shell.jpg)

### Cutting the Mini Crossword

The first lineup had a Mini Crossword. It showed the same clue every time, with no hints. A real crossword needs a fill algorithm and a clue database, and that's too much for one person.

So I cut it and put Word Search in its place: a new 8×8 board every time from a list of calm words, four directions, no timer and no way to fail. The gate can show up many times a day, and a puzzle that repeats is worse than no puzzle.

### Designing the failure state

The first Word Jumble could trap you. Get the word wrong and there was no way out, right when you were already annoyed. I wasn't logging wrong answers yet, so I only found it when the analytics showed a drop-off there.

![PostHog: the Word Jumble funnel](content/pause/mvql5muo-screenshot-2026-10-27-at-6.11.40-am.jpg)

What I changed:

- Retries are free
- After the first miss, "Show word" gives you the answer and then a new word
- Anagrams count as correct
- A "Mix letters" button to shuffle

If someone is going to get stuck, it'll be when they're frustrated. That's the screen I design first now.

![Word Jumble after the fixes, with Mix letters and Show word](content/pause/mvqlktxv-screenshot-2026-10-27-at-6.22.49-am.jpg)

### Working with what Apple gives you

Apple's Screen Time API is locked down on purpose. App names and icons come back as private tokens, categories can't be opened up to show the apps inside, and the system label ignores custom fonts.

Instead of faking a clean list, the dashboard shows app tiles and category tiles side by side. I found a layout order that gets the system title to match my caption size (give it room, scale it, then constrain it) and wrote the rule down in the code so a later change doesn't break it.

## 5. Seasonal themes

I wanted the app to feel alive and give people a reason to come back, without building a new app every season. The brief to myself: change the accent, not the app.

So I built a SeasonalTheme system (gradients, accent colors, fonts and decor) that resolves once on launch.

- **Halloween:** purple gradients, the Metal Mania display font, a moon, bats and webs, a new splash and puzzle thumbnails, and a Memory Match puzzle with a seasonal deck.
- **Thanksgiving:** a new theme and app icon, an embossed splash wordmark, and a Gratitude puzzle.

![The dashboard in its default, Halloween and Thanksgiving themes](content/pause/apps-season-theme.jpg)

Gratitude asks for three things you're grateful for, each at least 5 characters and all different. The answers stay on your phone, and later reminders quote one back to you. Analytics only log that you finished, never what you wrote. It's the puzzle where the pause is supposed to feel good.

A few rules kept it consistent: text on the gradient is white, cards keep dark text, and the code is the source of truth. The Figma puzzles are approximations.

## 6. Onboarding and the paywall

Onboarding is where my idea of the flow and what people actually got through were furthest apart.

The ads made it obvious. Most of my first downloads came from a $500 Apple Search Ads campaign, and PostHog showed where those people stopped:

- If you denied Screen Time or Notifications, you got stuck. Screen Time had no way back, because iOS doesn't put a Screen Time switch on the app's Settings page.
- A lot of people dropped at app selection, a system picker with no context at all.

What I changed:

- A "Try Again" button after a denied permission, and "Open Settings" where iOS allows it
- A Choose Apps screen before the picker: "Pick the apps that take up your screen time. Pause steps in before you open them."
- A shorter order: a primer, Screen Time (Step 1 of 2), Notifications (Step 2 of 2), then app selection
- A "Heads up" box that explains why Screen Time access matters before iOS asks
- Trial first: 7 days free, a reminder on day 5 (two days before it renews) that I disclose during the notifications step, and a free tier after the trial ends

![The new onboarding](content/pause/mvqlboxq-screenshot-2026-10-27-at-6.16.29-am.jpg)

Switching to trial first meant "No credit card" wasn't true anymore. It was in the Figma hero pills, the screenshot headlines and the end card of the preview video. I changed every one to "7 days free · Cancel anytime." A change isn't done if the screenshots still say something else.

## 7. How I work with AI

I built Pause solo, with Claude Code as my engineering partner. I own the problem, the taste and what ships. Claude turns my Figma frames into SwiftUI, reviews the code for risk, tech debt and drift from the design system, sets up the analytics, and checks that builds pass. I test everything on my phone.

The loop:

1. **Design it in Figma first.** Claude reads the exact frame through the Figma MCP, so nothing gets rebuilt from my memory of it.
2. **One thing at a time.** One puzzle, one screen, one detail per pass, so my review stays sharp.
3. **Test on my phone.** I send back how it feels ("too clunky", "looks great") with screenshots, and I make the call.
4. **Write the decision down,** so the next session starts with context instead of a re-explanation.

![Working alongside the simulator, with design feedback](content/pause/emulator-and-design-feedback.jpg)

Twice it changed what I did:

- I asked it to check my analytics and it found I was tracking the wrong things. `puzzle_reset` meant someone tapped Reset, not that they got the answer wrong. `upgraded_to_premium` fired when someone started a trial and never on a real payment. I would've planned the roadmap on bad data.
- When I moved to trial first, it pointed out that "No credit card" would be false everywhere it appeared. That's where the cleanup in section 6 came from.

AI made it cheap to act on my judgment. It didn't replace it. The question used to be whether I could build something. Now it's whether I know what's worth building and can tell when it's right, and that's still the design job.

## 8. Getting it in front of people

I also own everything that gets people to the app:

- **try-pause.com,** designed and built from scratch after I left Webflow, hosted on GitHub Pages. It's written in first person ("I built") on purpose. It's one person, and I didn't want it to pretend to be a team.
- **The App Store listing:** screenshot sets and a preview video for each seasonal release, plus keyword research.
- **Paid:** a $500 Apple Search Ads campaign.
- **SEO:** GA4 and Search Console, a canonical fix, an internal-linking pass, and blog posts comparing Pause with other screen time apps.
- **A public roadmap** where people vote on what I build next.

![try-pause.com in its Halloween theme](content/pause/marketing-site-halloween.jpg)

![The public roadmap, with votes](content/pause/public-roadmap-votes.jpg)

## 9. Results

Pause is early and the numbers are small. What matters is what they changed.

### Downloads went up, but not from keywords

Three weeks before and after v1.3, which changed the title and keywords:

| Metric | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Impressions | 775 | 1,840 | +137% |
| Product page views | 124 | 323 | +160% |
| Conversion rate | 5.67% | 6.45% | +0.78 pts |
| First-time downloads | 27 | 73 | +170% |

I wanted to credit the new metadata. But most of those downloads came from the Apple Search Ads campaign, and Applyra showed only 1 of my 13 tracked keywords ranking at all. So I stopped working on metadata and moved on.

I also noticed Web Referrer traffic showing zero while the site was live, so that tracking needs fixing.

![App Store Connect: acquisition, the latest view (newer than the three weeks in the table)](content/pause/appstore-connect-data.jpg)

![Applyra: keyword ranks stayed flat](content/pause/applyra.jpg)

### The real problem was week one

The paid installs made the math clear. It cost about $4.33 to get an install, and each download was worth about $1.14, so every paid install lost about $3. Paying subscribers were still in single digits. Buying more installs would only lose more money.

Marketing wasn't the leak. Week one was.

The number I watch now is D7 gate retention: people who open a puzzle 7 or more days after their first one. It's 16%. The target is 30%.

![PostHog: weekly retention by cohort](content/pause/posthog-roadmap.jpg)

### What I changed

- Removed the Word Jumble dead ends (section 4)
- Fixed the onboarding drop-offs (section 6)
- Cleaned up the data: an `is_internal` flag so my own testing doesn't count, a `first_launch` property, and subscription events that come from StoreKit instead of guesses in the app
- Set up the trial-first pricing test and wrote down what a win looks like before launch, so I can't explain the result away afterward
- Added onboarding session replay with text, images and the app picker masked, and updated the privacy policy and App Privacy label before it shipped

### What's next

Release 1.7 on Nov 1 is the test: do the Word Jumble fixes and the new onboarding move D7 gate retention? I'll update this with the numbers, even if they barely move.

## 10. What I learned

- **Design the failure state first.** That's where people are when they quit.
- **One system beats ten screens.** The shell is why 10+ puzzles still feel like one app.
- **Cut early.** Pause is better without the crossword.
- **Measure what you design.** Without onboarding data I'd still think marketing was the problem.
- **Stop when the data says stop.** The keywords didn't move, so I moved on.
- **AI made building cheap.** Knowing what's right is still the job.
